units.la: Ritum illud; Ingrato homine terra pejus nîl creat, vix ullas non feriit aures, sed quô minus me feriat totum, monet me Sapiens ille suo ναιρὸν γνῶθι, hanc arripere occasionem, quâ benevolentiam ac beneficentiam vestrā, quam hactenus expertus sum; maxime vero dum studiorum nostrorum fundamina jaciendi & sermonis Gallici addiscendi gratia ante aliquot annos extra Patrios ageremus lares, agnoscam; cum eam referre non valeam, imo omnia quae in me collata sunt, enarrare quam Sybillae folia mihi laboriosius foret. Adauget enim illum meritorum vestrorum erga me cumulum, quod beneficia collocaveritis in hominem planè immeritum & nec naturae nec fortunae dono commendabilem, qui, ut hebraeo utar dicendi modo, בן ארם praeter humanam & communem sortem praese ferret nihil, quo benevoli vestri affectus captaret auram. Quid! si memori revolvo pectore curas ac labores vestros, quos mei causa suscipiebatis; ubi diversa valetudine semel atq; iterum premebar sed tandem tamen Castigatoris Divini manum medicam experiebar, qui contra spem & Medici & omnium extremum morbi aculeum pharmacum mihi esse jussit, quo valetudine pristina restituerer: Illud divinae benignitatis, hoc vestrae humanitatis esse agnosco; quod in his valetudinarium meum cinxeritis lectum, me oratione ac ope sublevaveretis; Cum huic singulari gratiae ac humanitati vestrae, nullis officiis, nullo labore industriáq; mea me satisfacere posse videam, tamen cogitans nihil tàm ingrati esse animi, quàm dissimulare quòd debeas, cùm persolvere nequeas: decrevi debitum meum publicè fateri, quò sensum meum adversus vos atq; gratum testarer animum, ac saltem umbram solutionis sectarer, nam si officia officiis ac non voluntate potius, animóq; pensantur; fateor solvendo non sum: sin (ut Cicero putat) etiam cùm habetur gratia, in eo ipso quòd habetur, refertur; non vereor, quin sim, quae debeo, saltem animo ipso persoluturus; qui totus humanitatis vestrae merito debetur, totum etiam eum vobis addico; qui totus & nunc coeleste pulsat atrium, ardentissimisq; flagitat precibus; sit ipse, cujus thronum Angeli cingunt, Remunerator, Propugnator vester, qui vos apud Peregrinas Gentes versantes, diversaq; agentes, dum alius Parnassi montem, alius Martis campum iniret atq; graderetur, nunc Patriae reddidit, velit eivos quoq; servare, ut Majorum Laudatissimorum exemplo sic initiati, consecrati, exercitati. Amplissimorum vestrorum Parentum vestigia nostrae Reip. bono legere, premere & etiam justitiam Religionemq; unica Regiminis conservandi fulcra fovere, sectari aliquando valeatis, Ecclesiam Christi in qua enutriti, educati, defendatis, promoveatis, meq; vero, qui hanc Theologiae Explicationis ἀρχὴν sub vexillo Christi defendendam suscepi, vobisq; sacram esse volui, ex Clientum albo ne expungatis, sed porrò favoris vestri alas erga me explicetis, rogo.
units.tr: That saying, "Earth produces nothing worse than an ungrateful man," is heard in almost every ear; but lest it strike me entirely, that wise man warns me to seize the moment [καιρὸν γνῶθι], and to acknowledge the kindness and generosity of you, which I have experienced hitherto; and most of all while, some years ago, we were away from our native hearths in order to lay the foundations of our studies and to learn the French language. I cannot repay it, and indeed to recount all the favours bestowed upon me would be harder for me than the leaves of the Sibyl. For that heap of your merits toward me is increased by the fact that you have bestowed benefits upon a man wholly undeserving, and commendable neither by the gift of nature nor of fortune, who, to use the Hebrew manner of speaking, was "son of man" [בן אדם], and displayed nothing beyond the common human lot by which he might catch the breeze of your kindly affection. What! When I recall with a mindful heart the cares and labours you undertook for my sake, when I was once and again oppressed by varying ill health, yet at last experienced the healing hand of the Divine Chastiser, who, contrary to the hope of both physician and everyone, commanded that the final sting of the disease be a remedy to restore me to my former health: I acknowledge that the first is of divine kindness, the second of your humanity, in that you surrounded my sickbed with your attention and relieved me with words and help. Since I see that I can satisfy this singular grace and humanity of yours with no services, no labour, no diligence of my own, nevertheless, reflecting that nothing is so ungrateful a mind as to hide what one owes when one cannot pay it back, I have decided to confess my debt publicly, so that I may bear witness to my sense of obligation and grateful mind toward you, and at least pursue the shadow of repayment. For if services are weighed by goodwill and mind rather than by deeds, I confess I cannot pay; but if (as Cicero thinks) even when gratitude is held, it is returned in the very fact that it is held, I do not doubt that I shall at least repay what I owe in spirit itself. Since my whole self is owed to your humanity by right, I also assign my whole self to you, who even now knock at the heavenly court and entreat with most ardent prayers. May he himself, whose throne the angels surround, be your Rewarder and Defender, who, when you were wandering among foreign nations and engaged in various pursuits, while one went up the mountain of Parnassus and another walked the field of Mars, has now restored you to your country; and may he also wish to keep you as you have been initiated, consecrated and trained after the example of your most praised ancestors: that you may one day be able to read, press and cultivate the footsteps of your most distinguished parents for the good of our commonwealth, and to foster justice and religion, the only supports for preserving government; that you may defend and promote the Church of Christ in which you were nurtured and educated; and that you may not strike from the roll of your clients me, who have undertaken to defend this beginning [ἀρχὴν] of the explanation of theology under the banner of Christ, and have wished it to be sacred to you; but that you would continue to spread the wings of your favour over me. This I ask.

units.la: Theologia Christiana, est doctrina de Deo, ad ipsius gloriam & salutem nostram, cognoscendo & colendo.
units.tr: Christian theology is the doctrine of God, for his glory and our salvation, by knowing and worshipping him.

units.la: UBI notatur Definitum & Definitio; illud est Theologia Christiana; hæc continet reliqua.
units.tr: HERE the definiendum and the definition are noted. The former is Christian theology; the latter contains the rest.

units.la: Ubi in Definito notanda est vocis authoritas, quæ, quia αὐτολεξεὶ non extat in Scriptura, Ecclesiastica, non Divina, est. Æquivalentia tamen ejus est in scripturis. Eô referimus verba, quæ cap. 4. verf. 12. ad Heb. Vivus est sermo Dei ζῶν ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ. Quanquàm enim sint, qui λόγον ἐνδιάθετον intelligunt, de quo Joh.1. verf. 1. freti v.13. nec est ulla res creata non manifesta in conspectu ipsius : imò omnia sunt nuda & intimè patentia oculis ejus quocum nobis est negotium. Ubi filii Dei omniscientia notari videtur: nulla tamen est ratio, cur non λόγον προφορικόν in citatis verbis intelligamus; causa enim redditur in ver.13. ab omniscientia Dei desumptâ, cur scrutinium cogitationum & conceptuum cordis nostri sermoni Dei externo in ver.12. tributum fuerit. Æquivalentia vocis itidem est ad Rom.3. ver.2. ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τῦ Θεῦ. Quamquàm verum fit, quòd Johannes in Apocalypseos inscriptione à piis veteribus Theologus fuerit vocatus, quòd in asserenda Christi Divinitate primas teneret. Ita veteres in inscriptionibus Librorum Apostolicorum suo jure usi sunt, quemadmodum Epistola prior ad Corinthios cognomen ordiordinis, quô vocatur Prima, procul dubio ab Apostolo Paulo non accepit; Prior enim antequàm posterior esset inscribi non poterat.
units.tr: Here, in the definiendum, the authority of the word should be noted. Since the word itself does not occur in Scripture, it is ecclesiastical, not divine. Its equivalent, however, is found in the Scriptures. To this we refer the words of Heb. 4:12: "The word of God is living" [ζῶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ]. For although some understand the inward word (λόγον ἐνδιάθετον), relying on John 1:1, and on verse 13, "nor is there any created thing not manifest in his sight; rather all things are naked and laid open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do," the omniscience of the Son of God seems to be noted there. Yet there is no reason why we should not understand the spoken word (λόγον προφορικόν) in the words cited. For the reason given in verse 13, drawn from God's omniscience, why the searching of the thoughts and conceptions of our heart is ascribed in verse 12 to the external word of God. The equivalent of the word is likewise found in Rom. 3:2: "that the oracles of God were committed to them" [ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ]. It is true that pious ancients called John "the Theologian" in the inscription of the Apocalypse, because he held the first place in asserting the divinity of Christ. So the ancients rightly used titles of this kind in the inscriptions of the apostolic books. Thus the First Epistle to the Corinthians certainly did not receive from the Apostle Paul the name "First" by which it is called; for the first could not be inscribed before there was a second.

units.la: Vox Theologiæ sonat sermonem Dei vel de Deo; quæ duo conjungi debent, quia de Deo non nisi ex Dei sermone sermonicari licet.
units.tr: The word theology signifies the word of God, or discourse concerning God. These two must be joined, because one may speak of God only from the word of God.

units.la: Gentilibus, unde Theologiæ vox desumpta videtur, triplex erat Theologia; μυθικὴ seu fabulosa; φυσικὴ seu naturalis; πολιτικὴ seu Sacerdotalis. Illa Poëtarum; Ista Philosophorum; Hæc Sacerdotum erat. Illa in theatris; Ista in scholis; Hæc in templis colebatur. Hæc distinctio desumpta est ex Marco Varrone ut Augustinus testatur lib. VI. De Civit. Dei cap.5. Varroni ipse Tullius tantum lautum testimonium perhibet, ut in Libris Academicis dicat, eam, quæ ibi versatur, disputationem se habuisse cum Marco Varrone, homine, inquit, omnium facilè acutissimo, & sine ulla dubitatione Doctissimo. Quadraginta & unum libros scripsit antiquitatum. In fabulosò Theologiæ genere est, E g. quomodo Deus alius ex capite, alius ex femore, alius ex guttis sanguinis fit natus. Præterea quomodò Dii furati sint, adulteraverint, servierint homini. Denique in hoc genere omnia Diis attribuuntur, quæ non modo in hominem, sed in contemptissimum hominem cadere possunt. In genere Theologiæ naturalis, de qua multos libros reliquerunt Philosophi Gentiles, est, E. G. Dii qui sint, ubi sint, quod genus, quale, ex quonam tempore: an à sempiterno fuerint, an ex igne sint, ut credit Heraclytus, an ex numeris ut Pythagoras, an ex atomis ut Epicurus. In tertio Theologiæ Gentilis genere, est, E. G. quos Deos publicè colere, quæ sacra & sacrificia facere quemque par sit. Facilè ostendere est quòd sine ratione Varro fabulosum Theologiæ genus à Civili & Philosophico discreverit; id quod efficaciter ostendit Augustinus Cap. 7. Lib. VI. de Civ. Dei; quando inter alia inquit, numquid barbatum Jovem, imberbemque Mercurium Poetæ habent; Pontifices non habent? an aliter Priapus stat adorandus in locis sacris, quàm procedit ridendus in theatris? Laurentinæ sacra advertat, quæ Herculis erat scortum; vel sacra Junonis vel Cereris, Veneris, matris Deûm, ubi Atys, pulcher adolescens, ab ea dilectus & muliebri zelo abscisus, etiam hominum Ascisorum infelicitate deploratur. Hæc sacra, quæ in templis fiebant pudore absterritus exponere non audeo. De omnibus tribus Theologiæ generibus cum Apostolo exclamo ad Rom.1: 21. 22. Vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis & obtenebratum est cor eorum intelligentia carens; cùm se dicitent sapientes stulti facti sunt, ut Wollebius Gentilium Theologiam καταχρηστικὸς sic dici recte autumaverit. Contrà in Archetypam & Ectypam verè dividi potest; cujus distinctionis Author est Franciscus Junius, morem Platonicorum imitatus, qui Mundum alium Archetypum, alium Ectypum fecerunt. Archetypus est Authographum, vel typus primigenius, cujus imitamentum est Ectypus. Ita in Typographia archetypi sunt typi, qui excudendis literis sunt parati; literæ verò sunt Ectypus. Ita sigillum est archetypus; imago verò, quæ in cera ex sigillo relinquitur, est Ectypus. Vix reperire est in creaturis Archetypum, qui non alio respectu sit Ectypus. Theologia verò Archetypa, quæ est Cognitio, quâ Deus cognoscit seipsum, est absolutè Archetypa. Archetypa quidem vocatur; quia quæ Theologia est in Creaturis, illius est qualiscunque assimilatio vel imitamentum; unde Ectypa vocatur: Hæc distinctio Theologiæ, ubi à parte Cognoscentium consideratur, est æquivoca; ubi verò à parte rerum cognitarum, est analogica. Theologia Ećtypa vel est in Christo, vel in Cœlitibus, vel in Viatoribus. Quanquàm, ubi Christus Theologicè consideratur, in eo est Archetypa, ubi verò œconomicè consideratur, in eo est Ećtypa, de hac monet David Psal. 45:8. Propterea unxit te, O Deus, Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis. Itidem Johannes Cap. 3:34. Huic enim Deus non admetitur spiritum. Volunt Lutherani Theologiam Christi Ećtypam esse infinitam, propterea quòd humanæ ipsius naturæ omniscientiam attribuunt. Cui errori opponimus primò testimonium Lucæ, Cap.2:52. Jesus verò proficiebat sapientiâ & statura & gratiâ apud Deum & hominem. Quomodò omniscientia cum profećtu sapientiæ consistere posset? Novi Brochmannum regerere; quòd Christus homo, quâ homo, in statu Exinanitionis semper fuerit omniscius actu primo, sed non actu secundo; hoc est, quòd sapientiam cum crescente ætate magis magisquè usurpaverit. Respondeo; profećtus sapientiæ intelligi debet quomodò profećtus staturæ, in qua actum primum ab actu secundo nemo distinguet. Quid, quòd proficere sapientiâ ex vulgari usu sapientiæ acquisitionem majoris majorisquè, non verò sapientiæ acquisitæ majus majusquè exercitium denotat? Secundò oppono testimonium Marci Cap.13. 32. Sed de die illo ac hora nemo scit, ne Angeli quidem, qui in Cœlo sunt, neq; ipse filius, sed Pater. Quomodò cum omniscientia diei decretorii ignorantia conjungi posset? Regerunt Luth. itidem, Christum sapientiæ thesauros non semper in statu Exinanitionis usurpavisse. Insto, primò hæc explicatio est contra phrasin nescire diem illum. secundò eadem phrasis usurpatur de Angelis, in quibus diei decretorii ignorantia non est notitiæ neglećtum exercitium. Interim fateor, quòd nunc quidem Christus homo, etiam quâ homo, sciat & diem & horam, quoniam Christus homo, etiam quâ homo, venturus est ad judicandum vivos & mortuos; ut procul dubio ipse certus sit quando sit venturus; & crassa esset ignorantia in Christo glorificato, si ignoraret usquè adhuc diem ultimi judicii; quemadmodum crassius est ignorans Mercator, qui dies Nundinarum ex Calendario ignorat; crasse quoquè ignarus est ille Christianus, cui tempora Sacrorum Christianorum non sunt nota. Neque absurdum nobis esto quòd in statu Exaltationis majorem cognitionem Christus fuerit consequutus, ita docente Johanne Apocal. Cap. 1:1. Apocalypsis Jesu Christi, quam dedit ipsi Deus, ut indicaret servis suis, quæ oportet fieri cito. Oppono Tertiò Matthæi cap. 21:19. & Marci cap. 11:13. in quibus locis ostenditur duplex in Christo ignorantia, tùm quia ignoraverat in fico nullos esse ficus; tùm nondum esse tempus ficuum. Ridiculum est responsum Lutheranorum Christum hominem, quâ hominem, sciviisse in fico nullos esse ficus, sed scientiæ suæ vires non intendisse; intendit enim attendendo folia arboris, quæ è longinquo viderat, & ex iis augurando ficus.
units.tr: Among the Gentiles, from whom the word theology seems to have been taken, there was a threefold theology: mythical or fabulous (μυθικὴ), natural or physical (φυσικὴ), and civil or priestly (πολιτικὴ). The first belonged to the poets, the second to the philosophers, and the third to the priests. The first was cultivated in the theatres, the second in the schools, and the third in the temples. This distinction is taken from Marcus Varro, as Augustine testifies in book 6 of De Civitate Dei, chapter 5. Cicero himself gives Varro such a glowing testimony that in the Academica he says he held a discussion with Marcus Varro, "a man, he says, by far the most acute of all and without any doubt the most learned." Varro wrote forty-one books of antiquities. In the fabulous kind of theology belongs, for example, how God was born, one from the head, another from the thigh, another from drops of blood; also how the gods stole, committed adultery, and served men. In short, in this kind everything is attributed to the gods that can befall not only a man but the most contemptible man. In the kind of natural theology, about which the Gentile philosophers left many books, belongs, for example, what gods there are, where they are, of what kind and form they are, and from what time: whether they have existed from eternity, or are from fire, as Heraclitus believed, or from numbers, as Pythagoras held, or from atoms, as Epicurus held. In the third kind of Gentile theology belongs, for example, which gods it is proper for each to worship publicly, and what sacred rites and sacrifices each ought to perform. It is easy to show that Varro separated the fabulous kind of theology from the civil and philosophical without reason. Augustine effectively shows this in chapter 7 of book 6 of De Civitate Dei, where among other things he says: do the poets have a bearded Jupiter and a beardless Mercury, while the pontiffs do not? Or is Priapus to stand to be adored in sacred places otherwise than he comes forward to be laughed at in the theatres? Let him consider the Laurentine rites, which were the harlot of Hercules; or the rites of Juno or Ceres, or of Venus, the mother of the gods, where Atys, a beautiful youth loved by her and mutilated in female jealousy, is lamented even with the unhappy lot of the Ascisian men. These rites, which were performed in the temples, I dare not set out, restrained by shame. Concerning all three kinds of theology I cry out with the Apostle, Rom. 1:21–22: "They became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened; professing themselves wise, they became fools." So Wollebius rightly judged that the theology of the Gentiles is called so catachrestically (καταχρηστικῶς). On the other hand, theology can truly be divided into archetypal and ectypal. The author of this distinction is Franciscus Junius, who imitated the manner of the Platonists, who made one world archetypal and another ectypal. The archetype is the autograph, or the primary type, of which the ectype is the imitation. Thus in printing, the types that are ready for striking off letters are archetypes, but the letters are the ectype. So a seal is the archetype, but the impression left in wax by the seal is the ectype. Scarcely can one find in creatures an archetype that is not, in another respect, an ectype. But archetypal theology, which is the knowledge by which God knows himself, is absolutely archetypal. It is called archetypal because whatever theology exists in creatures is some kind of likeness or imitation of it, whence it is called ectypal. This distinction of theology, when considered on the side of the knowers, is equivocal; when considered on the side of the things known, it is analogical. Ectypal theology is either in Christ, or in the blessed in heaven, or in wayfarers. Although, when Christ is considered theologically, in him it is archetypal, when he is considered economically, in him it is ectypal. David points to this in Ps. 45:8: "Therefore God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows." Likewise John 3:34: "For God does not give the Spirit by measure to him." The Lutherans want Christ's ectypal theology to be infinite, because they attribute omniscience to his human nature. Against this error we oppose, first, the testimony of Luke 2:52: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." How could omniscience be consistent with an increase in wisdom? I know that Brochmann replies that Christ, as man, qua man, in the state of humiliation was always omniscient in first act, but not in second act; that is, that he used his wisdom more and more as he grew older. I answer: the increase of wisdom must be understood as the increase of stature, in which no one distinguishes first act from second act. Moreover, does "to increase in wisdom," in common usage, denote the acquisition of more and more wisdom, and not a greater and greater exercise of wisdom already acquired? Second, I object the testimony of Mark 13:32: "But of that day and hour knows no one, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father." How could ignorance of the day of judgment be joined with omniscience? The Lutherans likewise reply that Christ did not always draw on the treasures of wisdom in the state of humiliation. I press the point: first, this explanation is contrary to the phrase "not to know that day"; second, the same phrase is used of the angels, in whom ignorance of the decisive day is not a neglected exercise of knowledge. Meanwhile I grant that now Christ, as man, even qua man, knows both the day and the hour, since Christ as man, even qua man, is to come to judge the living and the dead; so he himself is no doubt certain when he is to come. It would be gross ignorance in the glorified Christ if he were still ignorant of the day of the last judgment, just as a merchant who does not know the days of the fairs from the calendar is grossly ignorant, and as that Christian is grossly ignorant to whom the times of the Christian festivals are not known. Nor should it seem absurd to us that in the state of exaltation Christ attained greater knowledge, as John teaches in Rev. 1:1: "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him, to show his servants what must shortly come to pass." I object, third, Matth. 21:19 and Marc. cap. 11:13, in which places a twofold ignorance in Christ is shown: both because he did not know there were no figs on the tree, and because it was not yet the time of figs. The Lutheran reply, that Christ as man, qua man, knew there were no figs on the tree but did not exert the powers of his knowledge, is ridiculous; for he exerted them by attending to the leaves of the tree, which he had seen from afar, and by inferring from them that there were figs.

units.la: Pontificii verò aliter sentiunt de humanæ Christi natu-ræ Theologia, quanquàm enim ei excellentem scientiam attribuant & rerum omnium vel quæ fiunt, factæ sunt, vel quicquid viribus naturæ præstari potest, tamen omniscientiam negant. Quibus opponi possunt superiora argumenta; nam iis non tantum ostensum est humanam Christi naturam non esse omniscìam; sed & Christum quædam, quæ fuerunt, ut de ficubus demonstravimus; & quædam, ex futuris, ut de die ultimi judicii ostensum, ignoravisse. Ad superiora nostra loca aliter respondet Bellarminus quàm Lutherani; à Luca quidem dici prosecisse, inquit, Christum sapientiâ,magis magisquè eam manifestando aliis. Sed retunditur itidem hæc explicatio, quia Christus à Luca dicitur non minus sapientiâ prosecisse quàm ætate. Ad locum Marci verò respondet Christum dici ignoravisse diem ultimi judicii ut notefaceret aliis; quæ explicatio subsistere non potest, quia dicendum foret, tùm & Angelos non nosse diem, ut aliis notefaciant, tùm Patrem verò nosse illum diem, ut aliis notefaciat; quæ quàm absurda sunt quivis videt. Pro infinitudine Theologiæ Estypæ, quæ in humana Christi natura, allegant Lutherani capitis 3. Johannis versum 34. ubi Deus θν ἐκ μέτρῳ spiritum Christo dedisse dicitur. Respondemus desumptam esse locutionem à consuetudine populorum Orientalium, ubi in conviviis ordinariis cuique convivæ suum demensum porrigebatur; in Extraordinariis verò omnia copiosissimè & confertim conserebant, ut Estheræ cap.1: 8. videre est: Constituerat Rex unicuique Magistro domus suæ, ut facerent pro voluntate uniuscujusque. Ita in ordinaria donorum spiritus distributione huic quidem per spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ; alii verò sermo cognitionis per eundem spiritum; alteri verò fides per eundem spiritum; alii verò donum sanationum per eundem spiritum; alii verò operatio virtutum; alii verò prophetia; alii verò discretio spirituum; alteri verò genera linguarum; alii verò interpretatio linguarum 1. Cor.12: 8. 9. 10. In extraordinaria verò donorum spiritus distributione, quæ uni Christo facta est, omnia dona spiritus, quæ in Ecclesiam unquam fuerunt collata, in humanam Christi naturam confertim & eminentiore in gradu effusa fuisse vult Johannes: Id quod Psalmista explicat Ps.45. per phrasin præ consortibus. Deindè Theologia Estypa quoquè est
units.tr: The Papists, however, think differently about the theology of Christ's human nature. Although they attribute to him excellent knowledge, namely of all things that are done, have been done, or can be achieved by natural powers, they deny that he was omniscient. The arguments above can be set against them. For it has been shown not only that the human nature of Christ is not omniscient, but also that Christ was ignorant of some past things, as we demonstrated concerning the fig tree, and of some future things, as shown concerning the day of the last judgment. Bellarmine answers our passages above differently from the Lutherans. He says that Luke speaks of Christ advancing in wisdom, becoming ever more manifest to others. But this explanation is also refuted, because Luke says that Christ advanced in wisdom no less than in age. As for Mark's passage, Bellarmine answers that Christ is said to have been ignorant of the day of judgment in order to make it known to others. This explanation cannot stand, because it would then have to be said that the angels too do not know the day, in order to make it known to others, and that the Father knows that day in order to make it known to others. How absurd these claims are, anyone can see. For the infinity of theology in the human nature of Christ, the Lutherans cite John 3:34, where God is said to have given the Spirit to Christ not by measure [οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου]. We reply that the expression is taken from the custom of the Eastern peoples, where at ordinary banquets a portion was handed to each guest, but at extraordinary feasts everything was served abundantly and heaped together, as can be seen in Esther 1:8: The king had appointed for every steward of his house that they should do according to each one's pleasure. So too in the ordinary distribution of the gifts of the Spirit: to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge through the same Spirit; to another faith through the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing through the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discerning of spirits; to another various kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues 1 Cor. 12:8, 9, 10. But in the extraordinary distribution of the gifts of the Spirit, which was made to Christ alone, John wishes that all the gifts of the Spirit that have ever been conferred on the Church were poured out upon the human nature of Christ together and in a more eminent degree. The Psalmist explains this by the phrase "above his companions", Ps. 45. Further, the ectypal theology is also

units.la: in membris Christi, quia Christus eorum est caput; ut Christiani inde vocemur, quia quemadmodum unguentum illud optimum superfusum capiti Aaronis, descendens super barbam, barbam Aaronis, descendit usque ad oram vestium ejus. Psal. 133. ita oleum gaudii, quod est Theologia Ectypa, superfusum Christo capiti nostro, inde descendit ad ipsius corpus, & quaslibet ejus partes. Quia vero membra corporis Christi in duplici differentia sunt; alia enim sunt in Coelis, alia vero sunt in terris; illorum Theologia est Theologia Visionis quia non amplius per fidem ambulant sed per aspectum 2. Cor. 5:7. & cernunt coram, non uti nos nunc per speculum & per aenigma 1. Cor. 13:12. Nec putandum est in terris a nobis Deum nullatenus videri; cognitione enim, qua Deum in his terris cognoscimus, apprehenditur ipsissime Deus; alioquin foremus idololatrae, quia adoramus quod cognoscimus. Annuere tamen scholasticorum Theologorum commento nolumus ex Theologia visionis concludendum esse putantium beatos fore Dei comprehensores, hoc est, Deum, quicquid est, esse comprehensuros: quanquam Thomas Aquinas addat explicationis gratia Deum non esse comprehensuros infinite quomodo Deus seipsum comprehendit: quae duo profecto se mutuo evertunt; quia enim Deus infinitus est, quomodo comprehendi potest, quicquid est, quin infinite comprehendatur? Nec juvat Thomam similitudo propositionis demonstrabilis, quae per aliquam probabilem rationem cognoscitur; in qua dicit non esse quicquam ejus quod non cognoscatur, cognosci enim subjectum, praedicatum, utriusque compositionem; totam vero non ita perfecte cognosci sicut cognoscibilis est. Parte Prima Quaest. 12. Art. 7. Qui enim per rationem probabilem demonstrationem dicitur cognoscere eam certè non cognoscit, & quicquid in ea est, non attingit; non attingit quidem connexionis robur, quanquàm attingat qualitercunquè connexionem. Nec juvat Scholasticos Johannes Apostolus 1. Cap.3:2. Scimus autem fore ut cum ipse factus fuerit manifestus similes ei simus; quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est. Ibi enim Apostolus non in eo est, ut curiosis & Deum ultrà quàm par est intueri cupientibus ingeniis pabulum quærat, sed charitatis divinæ contemplatoribus & admiratoribus satisfacit; & eorum fidem promissione sustentat fore, ut charitatem Dei penitissimè sint intuituri tota suæ salutis œconomiâ plenissimè patefactâ: Deus enim manifestus factus erit quandò charitatem suam, quâ in salute nostra inchoanda sustentanda & promovenda ardebat, familiarissimè beatis patefaciet; ex qua patefactione charitas Dei, quæ initia habet in viatorum animis, tantam perfectionem consecutura est, ut charitatis magnitudine beati visi fuerint absorpti; quæ mutatio Johanni est Deo similes fieri. Ut videre Deum, sicuti est, Johanni sit Dei charitatem, quæ in negotio salutis nostræ elucescit, familiarissimè intueri: hujus enim epistolæ utramque paginam facit doctrina de Dei charitate, quâ nos complectitur in filio; & doctrina de charitate, quæ unire fratres debet. Theologia verò, de qua in præsentiarum, non est Cœlitum sed viatorum; solet quoquè vocari studii vel stadii: vel, ut Author habet, est Militantium; quia adversus hostes nostros spirituales spiritualia nobis suppeditat arma, ut iis armati militemus & vincamus. Viatorum est, quia est loco vehiculi, quo per vallem lachrimarum vecti viarum molestias superare & patriam attingere possumus. Studii est quia ordinariè studiosâ diligentiâ acquirenda est; Theologia enim quæ in Modernis est Theologis, partim est acquisitus partim est infusus habitus, Apostolorum vero infusus erat tantum; ut ex historia Pentecostali videre est, ubi quanquam omnes donum linguarum subito acceperunt, tamen etiam Theologiam christianam repente imbiberunt; quia non tantum dicuntur linguis exoticis locuti, sed etiam magnalia Dei locuti Act.2. 11. quæ sunt magnalia Evangelii; ut ex postfacta concione Petri videre est; Piscatores, rerum rudes subito facti fuere summi Theologi. Paulus subito Theologus summus fuit factus ut videre est Act.9. ut, ubi Ananias Sauli impositus manus, subito impleretur spiritu sancto: eo enim fine Ananias ad ipsum missus, ut visum reciperet & impleretur spiritu sancto verf.17. Unde factum ut statim in Synagogis prædicaverit Christum verf. 20. inde ipse Paulus ad Gal. 1:1. Paulus Apostolus non ab hominibus neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum ac Deum Patrem, qui suscitavit eum ex mortuis; quanquam enim postquam Ananias impositus erat ipsi manus aptus illico ad exercendum ministerium Evangelii factus fuerit; Ananias tamen non missus erat ad illum docendum, neque illum docuit, sed ut Saul impositis manibus visum recuperaret & Spiritu Sancto impleretur. Nostra vero Theologia partim ad acquisitos, partim ad infusos pertinet habitus: ad infusos, quia lumine fidei saltem historicæ opus est sive Theologiæ principio sive conclusionibus sit assentiendum. E. G. Quacunque diligentia legeris, & meditatus fueris testimonia S. Scripturæ, quibus dogma resurrectionis mortuorum nititur, iis tamen non es assensurus, nec assentiri potes, nisi fidei ad minimum historicæ lumine donatus fueris. Ad acquisitos vero pertinet, quia Theologiæ principium est legendum, vel audiendum, meditandum, edişcendum, repetendum & diligenter exercendum: conclusiones etiam sunt labore inveniendæ, attendendæ, edifcendæ & tractandæ. Theologia verò Apostolorum omni respectu ad infusos pertinet habitus. Stadii est, de quâ Phil. 3: 14. Unum autem ago; ea quidem quæ à tergo sunt obliviscens, ad ea verò quæ à fronte sunt contendens, scopum versus feror ad præmium supernæ vocationis Dei, in Christo Jesu. Ubi de dogmatibus Theologiæ loquitur, sub parabola cursorum, qui quæ à tergo sunt non expendunt spatia, quia sunt superata, sed omnes intendunt nervos ut & quæ à fronte sunt considerent, & adhuc decurrenda spatia superent, & βεβαίου consequantur. Ita Apostolus quæ fidei dogmata probè intelligebat & quæ in iis erant contenta mysteria de novo meditari nolebat, neque ageret actum; contrà in scrutinio mysteriorum profundiore proficere voluit longius, ut consequeretur aliquandò scopum, hoc est, Theologiam metæ. Unde Theologia alia est stadii, alia metæ.
units.tr: in the members of Christ, since Christ is their head, so that we are called Christians from him. As that precious ointment poured on the head of Aaron, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, ran down to the hem of his garments, Ps. 133, so the oil of gladness, which is ectypal theology, poured on Christ our head, flows from there down to his body and all its parts. But since the members of Christ's body are of two kinds, for some are in heaven and others on earth, the theology of the former is the theology of vision, because they no longer walk by faith but by sight, 2 Cor. 5:7, and they see face to face, not as we now through a mirror and in a riddle, 1 Cor. 13:12. Nor should it be thought that God is in no way seen by us on earth; for by the knowledge with which we know God in this life, God himself is truly apprehended. Otherwise we would be idolaters, since we worship what we know. Yet we are unwilling to assent to the invention of the scholastic theologians, who, thinking that the blessed will be the comprehenders of God, conclude from the theology of vision that they will comprehend whatever God is. Although Thomas Aquinas adds, by way of explanation, that they will not comprehend God infinitely, as God comprehends himself, these two claims really undo each other. For since God is infinite, how can whatever he is be comprehended without being comprehended infinitely? Nor does the comparison Thomas makes help him, with a demonstrable proposition that is known through some probable reason, in which he says that nothing of it is unknown, since the subject, the predicate and the composition of both are known, but the whole is not known as perfectly as it is knowable (Part 1, Question 12, Article 7). For one who is said to know by probable reasoning, rather than by demonstration, certainly does not know it, and does not attain whatever is in it. He does not attain the strength of the connection, although he attains the connection in some way. Nor does the Apostle John help the scholastics: We know that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is, 1 John 3:2. For the Apostle is not concerned there to provide food for curious minds that wish to gaze on God beyond what is fitting; he satisfies the contemplators and admirers of divine love, and sustains their faith with the promise that they will look most deeply upon the love of God when the whole economy of their salvation has been fully laid open. For God will be made manifest when he reveals most intimately to the blessed the love with which he burned in initiating, sustaining and advancing our salvation. From that revelation the love of God, which has its beginnings in the souls of wayfarers, will attain such perfection that the blessed will be overwhelmed by the greatness of that love. This change is what John means by becoming like God. To see God as he is, for John, is to look most intimately upon the love of God that shines forth in the business of our salvation. For the teaching about God's love, by which he embraces us in the Son, and the teaching about the love that ought to unite the brothers, make up both pages of this epistle. But the theology with which we are now concerned is not that of the heavenly inhabitants but of wayfarers. It is also commonly called the theology of study or of the course; or, as the author has it, it is that of the militant, because against our spiritual enemies it supplies us with spiritual weapons so that we may fight armed with them and conquer. It is that of wayfarers because it serves as a vehicle by which we may be carried through the valley of tears, overcome the troubles of the road and reach our homeland. It is that of study because it is ordinarily to be acquired by diligent study. For the theology that the modern theologians have is partly an acquired and partly an infused habit, but the Apostles' was only infused, as may be seen from the Pentecost story. There, although they all suddenly received the gift of tongues, they also at once drank in Christian theology, for they are said to have spoken not only in foreign tongues but also the mighty works of God, Acts 2:11, which are the great things of the gospel, as may be seen from Peter's sermon after the event. Fishermen, untrained in matters, were suddenly made the greatest theologians. Paul was suddenly made the greatest theologian, as may be seen in Acts 9, where, when Ananias laid his hands on Saul, he was at once filled with the Holy Spirit. For Ananias was sent to him for this purpose, that he might recover his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit, v. 17. Hence it came about that he immediately preached Christ in the synagogues, v. 20. From this Paul himself says in Gal. 1:1: Paul an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead. For although, after Ananias had laid hands on him, he was immediately made fit to exercise the ministry of the gospel, Ananias was not sent to teach him, nor did he teach him, but so that Saul, with hands laid on him, might recover his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Our theology, however, pertains partly to acquired and partly to infused habits: to infused habits, because at least the light of historical faith is needed to assent either to the principle of theology or to its conclusions. For example, however diligently you read and meditate on the testimonies of Holy Scripture on which the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead rests, you will not assent to them, nor can you assent, unless you have been endowed at least with the light of historical faith. As acquired, however, it pertains to theology, because its principle must be read or heard, meditated on, learned, repeated and diligently practised; its conclusions also must be found, attended to, learned and handled with labour. But the theology of the Apostles pertains in every respect to infused habits. It is of study that Phil. 3:14 speaks: But one thing I do: forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. Here he speaks of the doctrines of theology under the parable of runners, who do not weigh the distances already passed, since they have been overcome, but strain every nerve to consider what lies ahead, to cover the course still to be run, and to attain [βεβαίου] what is sure. So the Apostle, who understood well the doctrines of faith and the mysteries contained in them, did not wish to meditate anew on them as if he were doing the same task again. On the contrary, he wished to advance further in the deeper search into the mysteries, so that he might at some time reach the goal, that is, the theology of the finish line. Hence one theology belongs to the course, another to the goal.

units.la: Regrediamur ad nostram Theologiæ Definitionem, postquàm satis perspectum esse putem de qua Theologia institutà sit nostra tractatio. Vocatur ab Authore Doctrina quia ut Præceptorum Systema consideratur. Præceptorum Systema est præceptorum colligatio, quæ singula & universa ad unius vel objecti cognitionem; vel finis consecutionem faciunt; illa in theoreticis; hæc in practicis locum habent. Ut quæcunque vel in theoreticis proponuntur præcepta, quæ cognoscendo objecto propositò non inserviunt: vel in practicis, quæ finis propositi consecutioni non inserviunt, propterea vocentur heterogenea: quæ contrà inserviunt, homogenea. Theologiæ Definitio, quomodò ab Authore proponitur, videtur ipsius verbi Divini definitio non probè attendenti; notandum verò vero quòd Theologia non sit ipsum Dei verbum; sed rerum, quæ sunt in Dei verbo, cognitio & enarratio. Si quis loquitur, loquatur ut eloquia Dei. 1. Pet. 4:11. Quandò Deus loquitur, loquitur verbum Dei: quandò verò homo loquitur, quod ipse Deus fuit locutus, & quidem fine salutari. Θεολογίζει.
units.tr: Let us return to our definition of theology, since I think we have now sufficiently considered what kind of theology our treatment is meant to be. The author calls it doctrine because it is considered as a system of precepts. A system of precepts is a connected body of precepts, each and all of which serve either the knowledge of one object or the attainment of one end: the former in theoretical matters, the latter in practical ones. Hence precepts that do not serve the knowledge of the object proposed, in theoretical matters, or do not serve the attainment of the end proposed, in practical ones, are called heterogeneous; those that do serve it are called homogeneous. The definition of theology as the author gives it seems to be a definition of the divine Word itself, to one who does not attend to it carefully; but it should be noted that theology is not the Word of God itself, but the knowledge and exposition of the things that are in the Word of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God, 1 Pet. 4:11. When God speaks, he speaks the word of God; but when a man speaks, he speaks what God himself has spoken, and indeed for a saving purpose. [Θεολογίζει].

units.la: Theologia, hoc loco, non ut habitus in intellectu residens, sed ut præceptorum Systema, consideratur, ideòque per doctrinam definitur.
units.tr: Theology, in this place, is considered not as a habit residing in the intellect, but as a system of precepts, and is therefore defined by doctrine.

units.la: THeologia etiam consíderari potest ut habitus; scilicet quandò est in intellectu & voluntate; & est facilitas cognoscendi & narrandi res, quæ in Dei verbo sunt contentæ finesalutari; sive est res ipsa, quæ in Sacra est Scriptura, quandò est in intellectu; sicut Apollos potens erat in scripturis Act. 18:24. Quæritur quodnam Genus ex habitibus intellectualibus ei sit assignandum? Notum est quòd Aristoteles quinquè fecerit habitus intellectuales, scilicet Intelligentiam, Scientiam, Sapientiam, Artem, Prudentiam. Intelligentia, est potentia sive vis intellectus naturalis, quâ principia tùm theoretica tùm practica innata habet; ita notitia quòd Deus sit adorandus, Parentes colendi, pertinet ad intelligentiam; quia nobis est connata. Scientia verò est notitia conclusionum, quæ ex principiis evidentibus & invictis lumine naturæ sunt deducta. Sapientia, est notitia augustior & sublimior, quæ est veritatum sublimium ex augustissimis principiis probatarum: ita demonstratio Existentiæ Dei ex principiis omni diabolicæ machinationis fraude superioribus facta pertinet ad sapientiam. Ars verò est habitus cum recta ratione effectivus; ut artis sit post operationem relinquere opus; quò pertinet ars architectonica &c. Prudentia est virtus, quæ hominis actiones dirigit, ut beatè vivat; est virtutum directrix; ostendit locum, tempus, speciem, personas &c. Ubi, quandò, quæ virtus, coram quibus sit exercenda vel non sit exercenda; ut regimini ipsius subsint omnium virtutum actiones; sic fit ut beatè in his terris vivamus. Ita fieri potest, ut qui virtutem fortitudinis habet careat prudentiâ, & sortitudinem exercere velit ubi nulla est necessitas. Ad nullum horum habituum Theologia restringi potest; luminis enim, quò utitur, dignitate superat omnes, quia cœleste & supernaturale est; principiorum etiam, quibus utitur, nobilitate superat omnes, quia ex singularissimâ Dei gratiâ sunt revelata; operationum utilitate artem tantùm superat, quantùm æterna salus præsentis vitæ commoda; conclusionum verò certitudine scientiam adeò superat, ut si quæ scientiæ sunt contraria doceret, credenda essent, quanquàm cum scientiæ detrimentò fieret. Quanquàm verò ad habituum intellectualium Aristotelicorum nullum Theologia restringi possit, omnes tamen in universum eminentissimô gradu quodammodò complectitur. Ex habitibus Aristotelis singulari jure putat Author Theologiam sibi vindicare sapientiam & prudentiam, propterea quòd principia tradit ex quibus conclusiones deducit, & simul hominis animum in actionibus suis dirigit; ita secundùm Wollebium oportet habitum Theologiæ partim speculativum partim esse practicum. Putamus difficultatem, quæ de genere Theologiæ, quandò ut habitus consideratur, moveri solita est, non posse tolli nisi prius dijudicata quæstione speculativus ne an practicus sit habitus Theologia? Hæc quæstio certè quidem non est logomachia, ex cognomentis enim de Theologiæ indole constare potest; ita compertum quoquè redditur, quæ quæstiones intrà Theologiæ cancellos contineantur, vel ab iis sint arcendæ; si enim Theologia esset merè speculativa, eæ quæstiones tantùm in ea tractari deberent, quæ in meram speculationem abeunt, exclusis illis, quæ ad praxin faciunt; contrà si purè practica sit, indè removendæ sunt quæstiones universæ, quæ ad praxin nullum habent usum: ut inde videre sit quòd plurimum interfit nosse ex utro sit genere an ex utroque. Quid quòd Arminiani omnes intendunt nervos, ut probent nostram Theologiam esse merè speculativam & ut hoc nomine eam odiosam reddant. Hanc quæstionem ut definiam, fateor, quòd ex Theologis sint, qui eam partim speculativam, partim faciunt practicam; imò sunt, qui quanquàm, ut Wendelinus, eam ex utroque genere constare permittant, ad practici tamen generis propiùs quàm ad Theoretici accedere fatentur; argumentis tamen utuntur, quibus potiùs probatur quòd sit tantùm practica. E. G. D. Marefius Loc. 1. §. 12. Syst. Theol. habet Mixtus etiam censendus est ex speculativo & practico: cum frustranea foret rerum sublimium, quas speculamur, notitia; nisi redigeretur in praxin, juxta illud Pauli monitum; intentus esto tibi ipsi & doctrinæ & permane in iis 1. Tim. 4: 16. ex quorum verborum intentione adeò non probatur mixtio ex utroque habituum genere, ut practicum genus tantùm inde probetur, quia monetur à Paulo Timotheus, ut quæ alios docet ipse ad vitæ suæ usum redigat; imo his suis ipsius verbis, cùm frustranea foret rerum sublimium, quos speculamur, notitia, nisi redigeretur in praxin, Maresius imprudens probat Theologiam esse tantùm practicam; Wendelinus verò hæc testimonia habet in suo syste: 1.Tim.1:5. finis mandati est charitas ex puro corde & conscientiâ bonâ & fide minimè simulatâ 1.Cor.8:3. Si quis diligit Deum hic edoctus fuit ab eo &c. His conatur probare magis ad practicum quàm ad speculativum habitum accedere Theologiam. Quanquàm probent quòd sit habitus tantùm practicus; quia & Maresius & Wendelinus & alii in suis probationibus frustrà præsupponunt, quòd sit ex genere speculativo, & quòd tantùm probationi locus quærendus sit quòd etiam ex genere practicô constet. Ego putem, quòd Theologia sit merè practica; quia omnis illius notitia ad praxin refertur. Unde 1. ad Tim.6. versu 3. doctrina vocatur secundùm pietatem; atquì pietas est Dei cum amore reverentia; ut ad pietatem omnia, quæ in Theologia tractantur, referenda sint, & omnes quæstiones, quæ ad Dei cultum nullum habent respectum, à Theologiæ communione sint arcendæ. Et qui eam partim speculativam partim faciunt practicam, inanibus speculationibus præsidium quærunt. Objicis primò; quomodò Theologia potest esse practica, cùm objectum ipsius sit Deus & res divinæ, ut opus creationis vel redemptionis; quæ non videntur esse θεωρητὸν τι. Respondeo Deus quidem suâ naturâ non est θεωρητὸν τι, sed ut est objectum Theologiæ; quia in eâ cognoscitur Deus ut glorificetur & ut colatur; atquì glorificare & colere Deum est θεωρητὸν τι. Ita res divinæ, quæ in Theologia ad discendum proponuntur, sunt media, quibus ad Dei glorificationem nostra pietas promovetur. Objicis præterea, Theologia non tantùm agit de praxi sed & de theoria. Ergo & Theoretica est & practa. Respondeo non quævis Theoria facit habitum practicum, ticum, sed quæ in nullam definit praxin. Quid in Theologia magis videtur speculativum, quàm hæ veritates? Deus est Trinus: Pater generat Filium: Pater & Filius spirant Spiritum Sanctum: & tamen, ut ipse Scotus affirmat, ad praxin sunt dirigendæ, quia fundamentum continent dilectionis in tres Deitatis personas tendentis. Objicis insuper, Vita æterna consistit in visione Dei; Ergo est tantum speculativa. Respondeo primò, Visio Dei, quæ privilegium est futuræ vitæ, est fruitio familiarissima, plenissimè manifestatæ Dei dilectionis; quæ referetur ad mutuam Dei dilectionem; ut suprà visum. Secundò, Visio Dei pertinet ad Theologiam metæ non stadii; de quâ in præsentiarum. Arminiani prætereà objiciunt nobis in suâ Apologiâ; vestra Theologia est tantum speculativa; quia praxis vestra nihil est, nisi pura puta Dei actio in nobis: nos boni sumus & bene agimus, quia Deus vi suâ divinâ ita operatur in nobis, ut non possimus non esse boni; nos mali sumus & peccamus, quia Deus non vult operari in nobis, &c. Ergò speculatores tantum estis. Respondeo primò falsum est nos tantum speculari; quandò enim Deus in nobis agit, nos agentes facit; ut Dei operatio nudæ & otiosæ speculationi non relinquat locum. Secundò, Peccat Apologia Arminianorum in ignoratione Elenchi, quia in hac quæstione non attenditur operatio, quâ convertimur in bonos, sed natura veritatum, quæ in Theologiâ proponuntur; quas ad unam omnes ad praxin esse ordinatas statuimus. Objicis tandem, ipse Wollebius sentire videtur, quòd Theologia ex genere duplici habituum constet; quia eam & sapientiam & prudentiam vocat, Respondeo distinctione facile componitur lis. Si Theologia tùm speculativa tùm practica vocatur propterea quòd in eâ res tractentur, quarum aliæ suâ natura cură sint speculativæ, aliæ verò suâ naturâ sint practicæ; quæ videtur esse Wollebii cogitatio, cogitatio est verissima. Si verò hæ denominationes tantùm à fine ultimo habitûs desumptæ sunt, Theologia est habitus tantùm practicus. Atqui denominationes à fine ultimo habitûs desumi & solent & debent. Id quod ex ipsa experientiâ demonstratur; nullius enim praxeos exemplum neque in Ethica, neque in Politica, neque in Oeconomia, quæ sunt habitus practici, ostendi potest, cujus cognitio vel speculatio non præcesserit. Ut non sine opprobrio Cathedræ Theologicæ quæstiones, quæ in meram speculationem desinunt, ad Cathedram Scholasticam; quæ verò ad praxin faciunt, ad Cathredam Ecclesiasticam relegentur; quasi verò in schola Theologica tantùm speculationes tractentur; quas tamen omnes à Theologiâ eliminandas esse putamus.
units.tr: Theology may also be considered as a habit, namely when it is in the intellect and the will. It is then a facility of knowing and reporting the things contained in God's Word for salvation; or it is the very thing contained in Holy Scripture, when it is in the intellect, just as Apollos was mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). The question is raised what kind of intellectual habit it should be assigned to. It is well known that Aristotle listed five intellectual habits: Understanding, Knowledge, Wisdom, Art, and Prudence. Understanding is the natural power or faculty of the intellect, by which it has principles, both theoretical and practical, innate to it. Thus the knowledge that God is to be worshipped and parents honoured belongs to understanding, because it is connate with us. Knowledge, however, is the knowledge of conclusions drawn from principles that are evident and invincible by the light of nature. Wisdom is a loftier and more exalted knowledge, of sublime truths proved from the most august principles; thus the demonstration of the existence of God, made from principles that stand above every trick of the devil's machinations, belongs to wisdom. Art, however, is a habit effective together with right reason, such that the work is left behind after the operation is finished; to this belongs architecture, etc. Prudence is the virtue that directs human actions so that a person lives well; it is the director of the virtues. It shows the place, time, manner, and persons: where, when, which virtue, before whom it is to be exercised or not exercised; so that the actions of all the virtues are subject to its rule, and thus we live well in this earthly life. So it can happen that someone who has the virtue of courage lacks prudence, and wishes to exercise courage where there is no necessity. Theology cannot be restricted to any of these habits. For in the dignity of the light it uses, it surpasses them all, since it is heavenly and supernatural; in the nobility of the principles it uses, it surpasses them all, since they have been revealed by the most singular grace of God; in the usefulness of its operations, it surpasses art only as far as eternal salvation surpasses the conveniences of the present life; and in the certainty of its conclusions, it surpasses knowledge to such a degree that if it taught anything contrary to knowledge, it would have to be believed, even though this would be to knowledge's loss. Although theology cannot be restricted to any of the Aristotelian intellectual habits, nevertheless it embraces all of them in general, in a most eminent degree. Of the Aristotelian habits, the Author thinks that theology rightly claims for itself wisdom and prudence, because it delivers the principles from which it draws its conclusions, and at the same time directs the human mind in its actions. Thus, according to Wollebius, the habit of theology must be partly speculative and partly practical. We think that the difficulty which is usually raised about the genus of theology, when it is considered as a habit, cannot be removed unless first the question is decided whether the habit of theology is speculative or practical. This question is certainly not a verbal dispute, for the nature of theology can be ascertained from its names. It also becomes clear which questions are to be contained within the bounds of theology, and which are to be kept out of them. For if theology were purely speculative, only those questions should be treated in it that end in pure speculation, excluding those that bear on practice; but on the contrary, if it is purely practical, then all questions that have no use for practice must be removed from it. So it is clear that it matters greatly to know whether it is of one genus or of both. Indeed, all the Arminians strain their sinews to prove that our theology is purely speculative, and so to make it odious by this name. To settle this question, I admit that there are some theologians who make it partly speculative and partly practical; indeed there are some who, though, like Wendelin, they allow that it consists of both kinds, nevertheless admit that it comes closer to the practical kind than to the theoretical; yet they use arguments by which it is rather proved to be purely practical. For example, Maresius, Loc. 1, §12, of his Systema Theologicum, says: Theology is also to be considered mixed, of the speculative and the practical, since the knowledge of sublime things which we contemplate would be futile unless it were brought into practice, according to that admonition of Paul: "Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine, and continue in them" (1 Tim. 4:16). From the sense of these words the mixture of both kinds of habit is by no means proved; rather, only the practical kind is proved from them, since Timothy is admonished by Paul to bring into the use of his own life what he teaches to others. Indeed, by these very words of his, that the knowledge of sublime things which we contemplate would be futile unless it were brought into practice, Maresius unwittingly proves that theology is only practical. Wendelin, however, has these testimonies in his system: "The end of the commandment is love out of a pure heart and a good conscience and faith not feigned" (1 Tim. 1:5); "If anyone loves God, he has been taught by him" (1 Cor. 8:3). From these he tries to prove that theology comes closer to the practical habit than to the speculative. Yet although they prove that it is merely a practical habit, Maresius, Wendelin, and others in their proofs wrongly presuppose that it is of the speculative genus, and that room must only be sought to prove that it also consists of the practical genus. I myself think that theology is purely practical, because all its knowledge is referred to practice. Hence in 1 Tim. 6:3 doctrine is called according to godliness; but godliness is reverence for God with love. So all the things treated in theology must be referred to godliness, and all questions which have no regard to the worship of God must be kept out of the fellowship of theology. And those who make it partly speculative and partly practical seek protection for empty speculations. You object first: how can theology be practical, since its object is God and divine things, such as the work of creation or redemption, which do not seem to be something speculative [theōrēton ti]? I answer that God, indeed, by his nature is not something speculative [theōrēton ti], but as he is the object of theology, since in it God is known so that he may be glorified and worshipped; but to glorify and worship God is something speculative [theōrēton ti]. Thus the divine things which are set forth in theology to be learned are the means by which our godliness is advanced to the glorification of God. You object further: theology deals not only with practice but also with theory; therefore it is both theoretical and practical. I answer that not every theory makes a habit practical, but only that which ends in no practice. What in theology seems more speculative than these truths? God is Triune; the Father begets the Son; the Father and the Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit. Yet, as Scotus himself affirms, these are to be directed to practice, because they contain the foundation of love tending to the three persons of the Deity. You object moreover: eternal life consists in the vision of God; therefore it is only speculative. I answer first that the vision of God, which is the privilege of the future life, is the most intimate enjoyment of God's love most fully manifested; and this is referred to the mutual love of God, as seen above. Second, the vision of God pertains to the goal of theology, not to its course, which is our present concern. The Arminians further object to us in their Apology: your theology is merely speculative, because your practice is nothing but God's own action in us. We are good and do good because God by his divine power so works in us that we cannot but be good; we are evil and sin because God does not will to work in us, etc. Therefore you are only speculators. I answer first that it is false that we merely speculate; for when God acts in us, he makes us act, so that God's operation leaves no room for bare and idle speculation. Second, the Apology of the Arminians commits a fallacy of ignoring the issue (ignoratio elenchi), because in this question attention is not paid to the operation by which we are turned into good people, but to the nature of the truths set forth in theology, which we all hold to be ordained to practice as one. You object finally: Wollebius himself seems to think that theology consists of a double genus of habits, since he calls it both wisdom and prudence. I answer that the dispute is easily settled by a distinction. If theology is called both speculative and practical because in it are treated things of which some are by their nature speculative, and others by their nature practical, which seems to be Wollebius's meaning, then the thought is most true. But if these names are taken only from the ultimate end of the habit, then theology is merely a practical habit. Now names are and ought to be taken from the ultimate end of a habit. This is demonstrated from experience itself: no example of any practice can be shown, in Ethics, Politics, or Economics, which are practical habits, whose knowledge or speculation has not gone before it. Hence it is not without reproach that questions which end in pure speculation are relegated from the theological chair to the scholastic chair, while those that bear on practice are relegated to the ecclesiastical chair, as if only speculations were treated in the theological school; yet we think all of these must be eliminated from theology.

units.la: Fateor quòd sint, qui in Scholâ Theologicâ quandoquè quæstiones inutiles & frivolas tractent & quæ cum praxi nullum vinculum habent; distingue Theologum à Theologiâ; abusus est, non usus. Ut omnium meritissimè, quanquàm & eminentissimè, meo quidem judicio, Theologia vocetur prudentia. Quanquàm verò in S. Scriptura quandoquè videatur vocari sapientia, quandoquè prudentia, quandoquè intelligentia ut Prov. 1:2. 3. Ad sciendum sapientiam & eruditionem, ad intelligendum dicta prudentiæ: ad percipiendum eruditionem intelligentiæ, justitiæ, jurisq; & omnis recti. Notandum est tamen, quòd talia & similia nomina in S. Scriptura laxè & vulgariè sumantur, & non ut in acurata habituum distributione sumi solent; ubi sapiens sine consusione habituum non potest dici scire sapientiam, neque intelligens dici potest intelligere prudentiam.
units.tr: I grant that there are some who in the theological school sometimes treat useless and trivial questions that have no connection with practice. Distinguish the theologian from theology: this is an abuse, not a proper use. For this reason theology may most rightly, and in my judgment most eminently, be called prudence. Yet although in Holy Scripture it sometimes seems to be called wisdom, sometimes prudence, and sometimes understanding, as at Prov. 1:2, 3: To know wisdom and instruction, to understand the words of prudence; to receive the instruction of understanding, justice, judgment and every right thing. It must be noted, however, that such names and similar ones are used loosely and popularly in Holy Scripture, and not in the way they are customarily taken in a precise distribution of the habits. There, a wise man cannot be said to know wisdom without confusing the habits, nor can an intelligent man be said to understand prudence.

units.la: ILle beatus erit Sapiens, qui pectore versat Scripturam Domini, nocte diequè vacans Lectura: sic te dicemus jure beatum Quem ad Sophiam Dîam Spiritus intus agit: Est verbum Domini tua nocte diequè voluptas, Ut nobis hodiè hoc perspicuè patefit, Sicquè tuo exemplo referes illum Sapientem, Quapropter cunctis jure beatus eris.
units.tr: That man will be a wise and happy one who turns over in his heart the Scripture of the Lord, occupied night and day with reading. So shall we rightly call you blessed, whom the divine Wisdom's Spirit drives within; the word of the Lord is your delight night and day, as we today have made this plainly clear. And in your example you will call him the wise man, therefore you will rightly be blessed above all.
Added out of honour and love.

units.la: Felicem populum prædico, qui sacro Ardore instituì Dogmatibus cupit Sacris, atque sacro Numinis impetu Divina militat pro Sapientia, Mortalium quæ gloria, Et Angelorum gloria, Deique summi gloriaCœlestis hæc Scientia.Felix Tuquè igitur, qui Sapientiam Hanc ambis stabilem, quam nequè secula Delebunt animis; quam nequè perdere Fortuna ulla queat; quam nequè callidiQuassabit astus Dæmonis. Non ambis: imò possides. Felix cui sic contigitPost ambitum possessio.Ast mirum fuerit, quòd labor improbus, Quòd constans pietas, quòd calidæ preces Divinam tulerint hanc Sapientiam? Cœlestem dederint hancce Scientiam? Deus suorum DogmatumArdore nostra pectoraInflammet, & laboribusAdsit piis & sedulis!
units.tr: I call that people happy which, with holy zeal, desires the sacred dogmas, and which, moved by the holy impulse of the Divine Power, fights for the Divine Wisdom. This heavenly science is the glory of mortals, the glory of angels, and the glory of the highest God. Happy, then, are you who seek this stable Wisdom, which neither the ages will destroy in men's minds, nor any fortune can lose, nor the crafty tricks of the demon will shake. You do not seek it; rather, you possess it. Happy is he to whom possession comes thus after seeking. But would it be strange if restless labour, steadfast piety and warm prayers had won this Divine Wisdom, and had obtained this heavenly science? May God inflame our hearts with the zeal of His doctrines, and be present with the labours of the devout and diligent!
